You can use wh-words in your sentences to form wh-clauses. The wh-words are who, whom, what, which, when, where, why, how, and that.
When you use wh-clauses, they can come after certain verbs like:

You can also use an object + wh-clause + infinitive structure.
  • My mother taught me how to sew.
I hope you know what a great place this is!
Do you remember which speaker talked about being convincing in an argument?
You can also use whether or if in wh-clauses to talk about situations where two alternatives are possible.
Whether is similar to if so you can use either when two options are discussed or thought about. You can also use whether or if when people are not certain about something.

Maria didn't know if/ whether she should invite Salvador to the wedding. He was her ex-boyfriend and he didn't like her fiancé. She was trying to decide if/whether inviting him would be the best decision.
We can use verbs like discuss, choose, consider, determine, think about, wonder, know, and debate when we want to talk about two or more alternatives.
I wondered if you heard me the first two times.
Well, I don't know whether I should follow such a silly rule.
Willingness, Annoyance, Refusal, Promises and Threats - A Review
You can use different modals when you want to show intention, willingness, refusal, and annoyance. You can also make promises and threats using modal verbs.

{"rows":5,"columns":1,"cells":["{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Willingness: you use the following modals to show that you are willing to do something. If ... will in first conditional sentences can also express a polite request.

I'll go with you to the doctor's if you want me to.
If you will cut up the vegetables, then I can make the chicken.\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Refusal: you use the modals when you don't want to do something. Other people and things can also show refusal as well. You can use if ... won't in first conditional sentences.

My boss will not give us a holiday on Boxing Day.
The bus won't start because something is wrong with the engine.
If Luis won't come to the party with me, I'll ask Jorge.\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Intention: this means that you want to do something. You use the following modals to express your purpose or aim.

I will send the e-mail now. (decided at the moment of speaking)
I'm going to spend my Christmas vacation in Barbados. (decided before the moment of speaking)
I would like to study medicine at university. (would like + infinitive)
I want to buy a swimsuit at the mall later. (want + infinitive)\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Promises: you can use the following when you make a commitment to do something in the future.

I will call you as soon as I get home.\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"Threats: use these modals when you want to threaten people or show that something negative will result.

I will tell your wife that you cheated on her.\"}"],"styles":" intro_table_border"}
So, Nancy, if you will allow me to ask, I'd like to know your thoughts about the Toastmaster's meeting.
a person who speaks in front of a large group
Example: If you will allow me to ask, I'd like to know your thoughts about the Toastmaster's meeting.
These are words you use when you give your opinion about a Toastmaster's club meeting.
the action of talking in front of a group of people in a formal setting
Example: In my view, it provides an opportunity to practice public speaking and you learn a lot by listening to the other speeches.
the person who runs a formal event
Example:  The master of ceremonies ran the meeting very well.
Example:  For Pete's sake!  That was too much.
a person who procrastinates (waits until the last minute to do something)
Example: Do you know why he is a procrastinator? I think it's because he doesn't like doing the things he has to do.
when no more time is left
Example: When I was a student, I would always do things at the last minute.
a person who speaks at a public event
Example: Do you remember which speaker talked about being convincing in an argument?

Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self-Assessment.

images.text:
Gareth: So, Tammy, if you will allow me to ask, I'd like to know your thoughts about the Toastmaster's meeting.
Tammy: It was interesting.
Gareth: Will you come back next week?
Tammy: No, I won't come back.
Gareth: I will be back for sure. I hope you know what a great place this is! In my view, it provides an opportunity to practice public speaking - you learn a lot by listening to the other speeches. Do you remember which speaker talked about being convincing in an argument? Was it the first or the second? He talked about using analogies.
Tammy: Yeah, he was very dynamic.

Gareth: Then there was the speech on the art of compromising. She was giving some helpful pointers, don't you think? I really believe it's hard to make compromises when I'm feeling angry.
Tammy: I didn't like the speech about procrastinating. I found myself disagreeing with the things that he had been saying. Do you know why he is a procrastinator? I think it's because he doesn't like doing the things he has to do.
Gareth: I don't know whether I should follow his example or not. I used to be a procrastinator, too. When I was a student, I would always do things at the last minute.

Tammy: Students will be like that. I liked the speech by the woman who went to China. I can't remember if I she went to Beijing or Shanghai. I would really like to have an experience like that.
Gareth: I will go with you. The guy who was backpacking in Chile had an incredible story. I was wondering where he got this story from.
Tammy: Remember the strange woman who didn't want to leave the stage? The master of ceremonies had to say: “If you won't leave now, I will ask for a security guard!”
Gareth: For Pete's sake!
